content:
Unsigned owner receives bank call saying scheme selected; bank says next day it was a mistake

The first deadline for owners of Wang Fuk Court to submit acceptance letters for the government's acquisition proposal ended on 30 June. Wang Chi House, where over 75% of owners are willing to sell their titles, has been included in the long-term residence scheme. The government said that as of the 16th of this month, sales agreements had been signed with 769 households.

Mr Chan, who lives on a middle floor of Wang Chi House, bought his unit in 2017 and has about HK$2 million left on his mortgage. He has not yet signed and returned the "acceptance of acquisition proposal letter". He told *集誌社* on Monday (13th) last week that day that he had received a call from a staff member at Standard Chartered Bank, which handles his mortgage, saying that the government had earlier notified them he had chosen "Plan B"—the option of taking the money and buying a new Home Ownership Scheme flat.

Mr Chan immediately said he had never signed or returned the acquisition letter, questioned that a mistake had been made, and asked to verify the information. The staff member read out his address, insisted it was government notification, and explained the mortgage arrangements after selling the title, also saying he would note Mr Chan's situation and inform his supervisor.

Mr Chan received a call from the same staff member the next day (14th), saying that after checking with the bank and reviewing the information from the government, it turned out the bank had "got it wrong"—according to government records he had not chosen "Plan B"—and apologised to him.

Worried about being 'represented', lack of information leaves him no reply

Mr Chan told *集誌社* that the reason he had not signed the acquisition letter was that authorities had not given any answers on maintenance fee arrangements, insurance compensation, or whether repairs would be carried out to allow residents to return to Wang Chi House to live. With too many uncertainties, he could not decide at this stage to sell his title: "It's not that you say sell and I sell." He believes the long-term residence scheme can only be decided by drawing lots, and the housing uses modular integrated construction with inconsistent quality, which does not attract him to sell his flat first.

After it was earlier announced that over 75% of Wang Chi House owners were willing to accept the acquisition, Mr Chan had already become suspicious. He said many people in the neighbourhood groups were not selling, and believed the relevant data was all "just what they say themselves," but "no one knows what goes on in the middle." He frankly said, "If they voted at the owners' meeting and announced the results immediately, then I would believe it." He also worried about being 'represented' and things being taken out of context, so he did not give any reply.

"No matter how I decide, I still have to sell to them"

Regarding the first call from the bank, Mr Chan was greatly surprised: "I never chose anything, but the government told the bank for me that I chose Plan B." He gave a wry smile: "So I'm one of that 75%. I always told people I'm not, who is that 75%? Turns out I am that 75%, and I didn't even know I had done it."

Mr Chan stressed that the fairest thing would be to vote immediately at the owners' meeting and then announce the results, but Hop On (Hap On / Hip On — *合安*? — the management company) had made clear the meeting would not deal with the sale of titles, and he questioned whether the authorities were "afraid that if there was an immediate vote there would be no way out." He sighed that this incident had made him feel even more that "no matter how I decide, in the end the government will use its methods to make me sell to them—it's just a matter of whether I sell earlier or later."

Even after the bank's call the next day saying it was a "mistake," Mr Chan's doubts have not been fully dispelled. He said, "That's what they say, that's what I hear."

Even less willing to sell after the owners' meeting

Mr Chan understands the scheme will not change, but he still hopes to find out whether, for Wang Chi House which has not been burned down, there could be an option of repairs to allow residents to return and live there. "As long as it hasn't been announced, there's still a chance we can really get it repaired." He also said that if the government ultimately legislates to acquire his flat, he will still have to sell, but if the government does not buy his title, "you still have to let me go back up and live there."

The owners' meeting was held on Sunday (19th). Mr Chan questioned whether it was legal, saying it was just "doing homework" and avoiding residents' questions—"it just says what it wants to say." Mr Chan said he would be even less willing to sell his title to the government after the owners' meeting, because insurance compensation could have been used to repair Wang Chi House, but after selling the title, the insurance would pay the government.

Housing Bureau: Cases with outstanding mortgages referred to banks after letters received

*集誌社* on Monday (13th) last week asked the Housing Bureau whether it was aware of the incident, whether the bureau had made an error, whether there were similar cases and whether this affected the data earlier announced, and how residents could be convinced. The Housing Bureau did not give a direct response, only replying yesterday (20th) that, according to an announcement by the HKMA and the Hong Kong Banking Association in March this year, the HKMA, the Banking Association and the banking industry would set up a communication platform, including through the Housing Bureau-coordinated "explanation team," to understand the specific needs of Wang Fuk Court residents and provide suitable assistance for each case.

The bureau said it has been maintaining close communication with the Banking Association and the banks involved in mortgages on Wang Fuk Court units. After receiving owners' signed "acceptance of acquisition proposal letters," the explanation team will, based on the mortgage information provided in the owners' letters, refer cases with outstanding mortgages to the mortgagee banks in accordance with the personal data collection statement contained in the letter, so that the banks can assign dedicated staff to contact the owners to help them understand the special mortgage arrangements provided by the industry to assist owners and provide appropriate assistance.

Standard Chartered: No comment on individual cases, handled with compassionate principle

A Standard Chartered Bank spokesperson replied on Tuesday (14th) last week that it would not comment on individual customer cases, saying it has always had a dedicated team that handles cases based on the individual needs of affected owner-customers of Wang Fuk Court with a compassionate principle, and ensures that customer data is properly handled.

The first deadline for acquisition at Wang Fuk Court ended on 30 June. Deputy Financial Secretary Wong Wai-lun said earlier that as of the 16th of this month, 1,786 households had signed and returned the "acceptance of acquisition proposal letter," accounting for over 90% of all households, of which about 43%, or 769 households, had signed the sale and purchase agreement.
